seo.whatIsAnswer: FractalPark is a free, open-source (MIT-licensed) fractal generator that runs entirely in your web browser. It lets you explore 94 different fractal formulas — including the Mandelbrot set, Julia sets, Burning Ship, Newton, Phoenix, and more — color them with 7 different algorithms, and export high-resolution PNG images up to 4× zoom, all without installing any software.
seo.howToHeading: How to Generate Your First Fractal
howToSteps: Open the Explore page and pick a formula — the classic Mandelbrot set is a good start.
Drag on the canvas to pan and scroll to zoom into the fractal boundary where the detail lives.
Switch to the Coloring tab and try smooth iteration, orbit traps, or a custom gradient.
Open the Render tab to enable SSAA anti-aliasing and adaptive iteration depth.
Click Export to download a high-resolution PNG, or Share to copy a link that restores the exact view.
seo.familiesIntro: Every formula is implemented in GLSL with both Mandelbrot and Julia modes. Click any formula name in the explorer to load it with sensible defaults.

seo.featuresHeading: What You Can Do with FractalPark
features: 94 GLSL fractal formulas with Mandelbrot and Julia modes
7 coloring modes including smooth iteration, orbit traps, and custom gradients
Real-time WebGL rendering at 60 fps on any modern device
High-resolution PNG export up to 4× with SSAA anti-aliasing
Shareable URLs that restore the exact view and parameters
Custom formula editor with AST validation and live preview

free.a: Yes. FractalPark is completely free and open-source under the MIT license. You can use it for personal, educational, or commercial purposes without any cost.

chinese.a: Yes. FractalPark is fully bilingual — both the interface and the content are available in English and Simplified Chinese.

export.q: How do I export a fractal as a PNG?
export.a: Open the Render tab in the explorer, choose a scale (1×, 2×, or 4×), and click Export. FractalPark will render the image at high resolution with SSAA anti-aliasing and download it as a PNG file.

formulas.q: How many fractal formulas does FractalPark include?
formulas.a: FractalPark ships with 94 fractal formulas organized into 7 families: Classic, Burning Ship, Newton, Phoenix, Transcendental, Magnet, and Exotic. Each formula supports both Mandelbrot and Julia modes.

share.q: Can I share a fractal I created?
share.a: Yes. Every view in FractalPark has a unique URL that encodes the formula, position, zoom, coloring, and all other parameters. Click Share to copy the link — anyone who opens it will see the exact same fractal.

opensource.a: Yes. The entire codebase is MIT-licensed and available on GitHub.
opensource.linkText: View the FractalPark repository on GitHub

index.title: Formula Atlas
index.intro: Explore FractalPark's complete catalog of 94 built-in formulas across seven families. Start with a canonical view, follow one of 21 in-depth guide profiles, or learn to write your own formula with FRM.

capabilities.title: One catalog, many ways to create
capabilities.intro: Every entry is derived from the same formula catalog and approved default state used by the interactive Explorer.

realtime.title: Real-time WebGL
realtime.description: Open any formula directly in the browser and explore its boundary with GPU-accelerated rendering.

canonical.title: Canonical starting views
canonical.description: Each destination is generated from the authoritative formula Document, including its view, parameters, and coloring.

server.title: Server-readable directory
server.description: All seven families and 94 destinations remain available in the initial HTML without client-side search or filtering.

families.title: Choose a mathematical character
families.intro: Families organize formulas by their iteration structure and visual behavior. Counts come directly from the current built-in catalog.

descriptions.classic: Quadratic, polynomial, Julia, multicorn, and related escape-time foundations.
descriptions.burning-ship: Folded absolute-value maps with sharp hulls, ridges, and flame-like boundaries.
descriptions.newton: Convergent root-finding systems that divide the plane into colored basins.
descriptions.magnet: Rational maps with poles, dense boundaries, and magnetic basin structures.
descriptions.phoenix: Memory-dependent iterations whose previous orbit state shapes the next step.
descriptions.transcendental: Exponential, trigonometric, hyperbolic, and logarithmic complex maps.
descriptions.exotic: Reciprocal, rational, inversion, tetration, and other hybrid constructions.

frm.title: Learn and write formulas with FRM
frm.description: FRM is FractalPark's tested text-based authoring path. Read the compatibility guide, study compile-checked examples, then write and preview a formula locally in the standalone editor.

guides.title: In-depth guide set
guides.intro: These formulas are the frozen guide set selected from FractalPark's published artwork. Four validation guides are now available; the remaining canonical views stay ready to explore while their editorial pages are completed.

directory.title: All 94 formulas
directory.intro: The full directory is grouped by family and rendered on the server. Every link opens the formula with its canonical localized Explorer state.

cta.title: Start from a formula or write your own
cta.description: Use the Explorer for built-in formulas, or open the local FRM Editor when you want to define the iteration yourself.

remix.title: Start from the canonical Document
remix.description: Open the same approved formula state used by this guide, then change the view, coloring, transforms, or animation in the interactive Explorer.

frmGuide.title: Write Fractals with FRM
frmGuide.intro: Learn FractalPark's tested FRM subset, understand how source becomes a GPU shader, and build three working formulas from the same examples used by the editor.

what-is-frm.title: What Is FRM
body: FRM is a compact, text-based way to describe an iterative fractal. A formula names its starting state, the calculation repeated for each orbit, and the condition that decides whether iteration continues.

The format grew out of the Fractint ecosystem, where formula files made it possible to exchange experiments without rebuilding the rendering program. FractalPark carries that authoring idea into a browser workflow while documenting its own tested subset instead of claiming complete compatibility.
what-is-frm.historyPrefix: For the wider project's origins and history, see the

support.title: FRM Support in FractalPark
support.intro: FractalPark tokenizes, parses, validates, and compiles a deliberate FRM subset. The table separates constructs that work directly, constructs with documented FractalPark semantics, and constructs the current workflow cannot preserve.

supported.label: Supported
supported.meaning: Covered by compiler tests and usable without a semantic qualification.

adapted.label: Adapted
adapted.meaning: Accepted with a documented semantic difference or as a FractalPark extension.

unsupported.label: Unsupported
unsupported.meaning: Not preserved by the current compiler or file workflow; rejected rather than silently rewritten.

items.single-formula: One formula declaration per source document
items.expressions: Real and complex literals; arithmetic, comparison, logical, unary, and magnitude expressions
items.builtins: z, c, pixel, zPrev, p1–p5, constants, and tested built-in functions
items.diagnostics: Structured diagnostics and FRM-to-GLSL source mapping
items.ismand: ismand maps to FractalPark's current Mandelbrot/Julia runtime mode
items.native-directives: @mode: native, @default-view, and @default-coloring are FractalPark extensions; default directives apply only in native mode
items.multi-formula-files: Selecting among multiple formulas in one file
items.dialect-conversion: Automatic conversion of classic Fractint dialects
items.rejected-constructs: Any construct rejected by the current compile pipeline

support.disclaimer: This is a tested compatibility baseline, not a claim of full Fractint compatibility. When the compiler changes, this matrix and its tests must change together.

anatomy.title: Formula Anatomy
anatomy.intro: A FractalPark FRM formula has one named declaration and three explicit sections. Together they define the state transition for every pixel.

parts.init: Runs once for a pixel. Set the initial orbit value and any helper variables here.
parts.loop: Runs once per iteration. Update z and any state that the next iteration needs.
parts.bailout: Returns the condition for continuing the orbit. When it becomes false, the point has escaped.

anatomy.note: The section names are structural, not comments: omitting or misspelling one produces a diagnostic.

syntax.title: Syntax Guide
syntax.intro: The language stays intentionally small: expressions describe complex arithmetic, statements update orbit state, and control flow selects among updates.

sections.title: Declaration and sections
sections.body: Wrap one named formula in braces, then write init:, loop:, and bailout: in that order.

values.title: Values and variables
values.body: Use real numbers such as 0.15, complex pairs such as (0.05, -0.02), built-in orbit values, or your own assigned variables.

operators.title: Expressions
operators.body: Arithmetic, powers, comparisons, logical operators, unary operators, |z| magnitude syntax, and tested complex functions can be combined.

control-flow.title: Control flow
control-flow.body: Use if, elseif, else, and endif when an orbit update depends on a condition. Blocks must be balanced.

builtins.title: Built-ins
builtins.body: Core names include z, c, pixel, zPrev, p1–p5, pi, e, maxit, ismand, fn1–fn4, and the functions covered by compiler tests.

comments.title: Comments and directives
comments.body: Semicolon comments document source. Recognized @ directives configure FractalPark native behavior; unknown directives are not silently ignored.

pipeline.title: FRM to AST to GLSL Pipeline
pipeline.intro: FractalPark does not paste FRM text into a shader. It passes source through a staged compiler so syntax, meaning, generated code, and diagnostics stay connected.

source.title: FRM source
source.body: The exact text from the editor, paste, or local file is the authoritative input.

tokens.title: Lexer tokens
tokens.body: The lexer recognizes names, numbers, operators, section markers, comments, and directives while retaining source locations.

ast.title: Parsed AST
ast.body: The parser builds a structured formula tree and reports malformed declarations, expressions, and control-flow blocks.

validation.title: Validation and canonical form
validation.body: The validator checks names, types, sections, and supported semantics before a canonical formula is created.

glsl.title: GLSL and source map
glsl.body: Code generation emits shader functions and records mappings from generated GLSL back to FRM source.

plugin.title: Formula plugin
plugin.body: A successful compile becomes the same formula-plugin contract used by the renderer and shader assembly system.

pipeline.note: The shared compiler contract keeps Explore, the standalone Editor, saved custom formulas, examples, and tests on one implementation path.

tutorials.title: Progressive Tutorials
tutorials.intro: These examples advance from the smallest quadratic formula to parameters and stateful feedback. Each source block is taken directly from the shared example registry and compiled during tests.

goals.starter-brot: Focus: the declaration and the init / loop / bailout structure. Change the exponent or escape threshold only after this version compiles.
goals.parameter-drift: Focus: p1 and p2 parameter slots, a complex literal, and cabs(z) as an explicit magnitude function.
goals.orbit-echo: Focus: zPrev as the previous orbit state. Feedback adds memory without introducing a second manually managed state variable.

tutorials.editorNote: The FRM Editor opens these same compile-checked examples by stable ID. Formula source remains local and is never embedded in the URL.

diagnostics.title: Errors and Diagnostics
diagnostics.intro: Compilation stops at the earliest unsafe stage and reports source-oriented messages. A rejected construct is never rewritten into something that merely looks similar.

lexer.title: Lexical errors
lexer.body: Unexpected characters and unsupported identifiers are reported with their line and column.

parser.title: Parse errors
parser.body: Malformed sections, expressions, or control-flow blocks are diagnosed before semantic validation.

validator.title: Validation errors
validator.body: Unknown variables, invalid assignments, type mismatches, and unsupported semantics prevent code generation.

source-map.title: Shader source mapping
source-map.body: Generated GLSL retains mappings that can point a shader compilation failure back to the originating FRM location.

diagnostics.note: When fixing an error, start with the first reported message: later diagnostics can be consequences of the same missing token or invalid expression.

next-steps.title: Examples, Next Steps, and References
next-steps.exploreBody: Open Explore to compare built-in formula behavior, coloring, transforms, animation, and export controls before writing a custom formula.
next-steps.editorNote: Use the dedicated FRM Editor to compile, preview, import, download, and save local formulas before handing one off to Explore.
next-steps.referencesIntro: Historical context and implementation details are linked separately so the guide can distinguish the Fractint lineage from FractalPark's current compiler contract.

mandelbrot.title: Mandelbrot Set
mandelbrot.summary: The foundational quadratic parameter set, built by testing which complex values keep an orbit bounded.
mandelbrot.overview: The Mandelbrot set treats each point in the complex plane as the parameter c and follows the orbit from z = 0. Its simple recurrence produces a connected map of stable regions and an endlessly detailed boundary, making it a practical starting point for understanding escape-time fractals.
mandelbrot.imageAlt: Canonical FractalPark rendering of the Mandelbrot set
mandelbrot.imageCaption: The approved canonical Mandelbrot Document rendered by FractalPark.

iteration.label: Quadratic iteration
iteration.explanation: Start at zero and repeatedly square the current value before adding the fixed complex parameter c.

mandelbrot.visualCharacteristics: A cardioid-shaped body opens into bulbs, filaments, spirals, and repeating miniature copies along its boundary.

membership.question: What decides whether a point belongs to the Mandelbrot set?
membership.answer: A parameter belongs when its orbit, starting from zero, remains bounded under repeated quadratic iteration.

julia-mode.question: How is a Julia set related to this formula?
julia-mode.answer: A Julia set fixes c and varies the starting point, while the Mandelbrot set varies c from a fixed starting point.

lambda.title: Lambda Fractal
lambda.summary: A complex logistic map whose parameter controls the multiplication and folding of each orbit.

iteration.label: Complex logistic iteration
iteration.explanation: FractalPark offsets the stored orbit by one half, multiplies the two complementary factors, and scales them by c.

lambda.visualCharacteristics: Rounded lobes, branching channels, and vortex-like Julia structures appear as the complex multiplier changes.

parameter-role.question: What does lambda control?
parameter-role.answer: Lambda is the complex multiplier that changes both the growth and rotation of the orbit.

julia-mode.question: Why does Julia mode look especially varied?
julia-mode.answer: Fixing a complex lambda exposes the boundary between starting points with different long-term behavior.

mandelbox.title: Mandelbox
mandelbox.summary: A two-dimensional Mandelbox-inspired map that alternates box and radial folds before scaling the orbit.
mandelbox.overview: FractalPark's Mandelbox formula adapts the fold-and-scale idea to a two-dimensional complex-plane renderer. Box folds reflect coordinates, a radial fold changes scale around the origin, and repeated application builds a map with unusually architectural depth.
mandelbox.imageAlt: Canonical FractalPark rendering of the two-dimensional Mandelbox-inspired map
mandelbox.imageCaption: The approved canonical Mandelbox Document rendered by FractalPark.

iteration.label: Fold-and-scale iteration
iteration.explanation: The orbit is folded against a box, folded again by radius, scaled, and then translated by c.

mandelbox.visualCharacteristics: Hard-edged chambers, nested fortifications, and dimensional-looking corridors emerge from repeated folds.

parameters.scale: Scale controls how strongly the folded orbit expands or reverses before c is added.

folds.question: What are box and ball folds?
folds.answer: They are geometric transformations that reflect coordinates across box boundaries and rescale points by radius.

dimension.question: Is this the three-dimensional Mandelbox?
dimension.answer: No. FractalPark renders a two-dimensional map inspired by the same fold-and-scale construction.

perpendicular-celtic.title: Perpendicular Celtic
perpendicular-celtic.summary: A folded quadratic map that applies absolute values before and after squaring to create interlocking structure.

iteration.label: Perpendicular Celtic iteration
iteration.explanation: The real input is folded, the complex value is squared, and the resulting real component is folded again.

perpendicular-celtic.visualCharacteristics: Braided bands, mirrored arches, and porcelain-like loops form around sharply folded boundaries.

folding.question: Why are absolute values used twice?
folding.answer: The two folds alter different stages of the quadratic map and create its characteristic interlocking symmetry.

symmetry.question: Is it simply a rotated Burning Ship?
symmetry.answer: No. Its component folds occur in a different order, so its orbit geometry and symmetries are distinct.

quartic-julia.title: Quartic Julia
quartic-julia.summary: A fourth-degree Julia-family map in which each iteration raises z to the fourth power before adding c.

iteration.label: Quartic iteration
iteration.explanation: The fourth power multiplies angular structure and produces fourfold tendencies around many features.

quartic-julia.visualCharacteristics: Fine seals, branching rosettes, and four-way filament systems replace the quadratic family's simpler branching.

name.question: Why is this called Quartic Julia?
name.answer: Its iteration uses z to the fourth power; the public name states that degree explicitly.

constant.question: What does c change?
constant.answer: The fixed complex constant c determines the connectedness, symmetry, and detailed shape of the Julia set.

burning-ship.title: Burning Ship
burning-ship.summary: A quadratic escape-time fractal that folds both coordinate components before squaring.
burning-ship.overview: The Burning Ship changes the familiar quadratic recurrence by taking the absolute value of both coordinate components before each square. That small fold removes the Mandelbrot set's balance and creates steep ridges, repeated ship-like silhouettes, and strongly directional detail.
burning-ship.imageAlt: Canonical FractalPark rendering of the Burning Ship fractal
burning-ship.imageCaption: The approved canonical Burning Ship Document rendered by FractalPark.

iteration.label: Absolute-value quadratic iteration
iteration.explanation: Both real and imaginary components are made nonnegative before the usual quadratic step.

burning-ship.visualCharacteristics: Dark ship-like silhouettes sit above layered ridges, chimneys, and highly asymmetric coastal detail.

difference.question: How does it differ from the Mandelbrot set?
difference.answer: The component-wise absolute value breaks the Mandelbrot set's rotational balance and creates a distinct folded boundary.

orientation.question: Why can the ship appear upside down?
orientation.answer: Screen coordinates and artistic rotation can change its displayed orientation without changing the underlying set.

airship.title: Airship
airship.summary: A Burning Ship relative with an asymmetric coordinate fold that reshapes the quadratic orbit.

iteration.label: Airship fold
iteration.explanation: The real component is folded while the imaginary component couples x to the absolute value of y.

airship.visualCharacteristics: Wing-like lobes and airborne silhouettes stretch from narrow seams, especially under spatial transforms.

folding.question: How is the Airship fold different?
folding.answer: It folds x directly and builds the other coordinate from x times the absolute value of y instead of folding both independently.

transform.question: Does the formula require an inversion transform?
transform.answer: No. Inversion can create striking compositions, but the Airship formula is complete without a view transform.

newton-3.title: Newton Fractal for z³ − 1
newton-3.summary: A convergence fractal that applies Newton's root-finding method to the three roots of z cubed minus one.
newton-3.overview: Instead of asking whether an orbit escapes, this formula asks which root of z³ − 1 Newton's method reaches from each starting point. The resulting three basins are easy to identify, while their shared boundary reveals extreme sensitivity to the initial value.
newton-3.imageAlt: Canonical FractalPark rendering of the Newton fractal for z cubed minus one
newton-3.imageCaption: The approved canonical Newton 3 Document rendered by FractalPark.

iteration.label: Newton iteration
iteration.explanation: Each step subtracts the polynomial value divided by its derivative, moving z toward a root.

newton-3.visualCharacteristics: Three colored basins meet along infinitely intricate boundaries filled with spirals and repeated root patterns.

basins.question: What do the main regions represent?
basins.answer: Each basin contains starting points that converge to the same one of the polynomial's three roots.

escape.question: Is this an escape-time fractal?
escape.answer: It is primarily a convergence fractal, classified by which root an orbit approaches and how quickly.

newton-cosh.title: Newton Cosh
newton-cosh.summary: Newton's method applied to the transcendental equation cosh z equals one.

iteration.label: Newton iteration for cosh
iteration.explanation: The correction divides cosh(z) minus one by sinh(z), the derivative of cosh.

newton-cosh.visualCharacteristics: Repeating horizontal root bands bend into fine meridians and complex basin boundaries.

target.question: What equation is being solved?
target.answer: The iteration seeks complex solutions of cosh(z) = 1.

singularities.question: Why are some regions extremely sensitive?
singularities.answer: The Newton correction becomes unstable near points where sinh(z), the denominator, is close to zero.

magnet-type-1.title: Magnet Type 1
magnet-type-1.summary: A rational map whose squared quotient produces dense magnetic-looking basins and orbit chains.

iteration.label: Type 1 rational iteration
iteration.explanation: The orbit squares the ratio between z plus c and z minus c.

magnet-type-1.visualCharacteristics: Compact cores trail bead-like chains, spores, and nested rings around sharp rational-map boundaries.

name.question: Why is it called Magnet?
name.answer: The traditional name reflects the clustered, field-like appearance of many rendered parameter choices.

poles.question: What happens near z = c?
poles.answer: The denominator approaches zero, creating a pole that strongly redirects nearby orbits.

magnet-type-2.title: Magnet Type 2
magnet-type-2.summary: A second rational Magnet map that places z squared in both parts of the defining quotient.

iteration.label: Type 2 rational iteration
iteration.explanation: Square z first, form the ratio with plus and minus c, and square that ratio again.

magnet-type-2.visualCharacteristics: Crosses, reefs, rings, and tightly packed lobes appear with stronger repeated symmetry than Type 1.

difference.question: How does Type 2 differ from Type 1?
difference.answer: Type 2 uses z squared inside the quotient, adding another layer of symmetry and nonlinear folding.

poles.question: Where do its poles occur?
poles.answer: Poles occur where z squared equals c, so their positions depend on the square roots of the parameter.

multi-phoenix.title: Multi-Phoenix
multi-phoenix.summary: A memory-dependent quadratic recurrence that feeds the previous orbit value into the next step.

iteration.label: Phoenix recurrence
iteration.explanation: In addition to z squared and c, each step adds the previous z value multiplied by p.

multi-phoenix.visualCharacteristics: Feathered spokes, flame-like fans, and compass structures emerge from the recurrence's one-step memory.

parameters.memory: The memory coefficient p controls the strength and direction of the previous orbit value's influence.

memory.question: Why does this formula need the previous value?
memory.answer: The recurrence is second-order: its next state depends on both the current and immediately preceding orbit values.

initial-state.question: Does the initial previous value matter?
initial-state.answer: Yes. The recurrence must define both its current and previous starting states for deterministic behavior.

cosh-mandelbrot.title: Cosh Mandelbrot
cosh-mandelbrot.summary: A transcendental escape-time map that replaces polynomial squaring with the complex hyperbolic cosine.

iteration.label: Hyperbolic cosine iteration
iteration.explanation: Each step evaluates complex cosh at the current orbit value and then adds c.

cosh-mandelbrot.visualCharacteristics: Periodic plumes, layered fans, and repeating vertical structures reflect the transcendental function's growth.

periodicity.question: Why do patterns repeat vertically?
periodicity.answer: Complex hyperbolic cosine is periodic in the imaginary direction, so related orbit structures recur.

growth.question: Why do many points escape rapidly?
growth.answer: The exponential terms inside cosh can grow very quickly for parts of the complex plane.

buffalo.title: Buffalo
buffalo.summary: A folded quadratic variant that combines absolute coordinate squares with a signed cross term.

iteration.label: Buffalo iteration
iteration.explanation: The squared coordinate magnitudes form the real part while the imaginary part keeps x and folds y.

buffalo.visualCharacteristics: Horned crests, eclipses, and mirrored gates grow from broad folded lobes.

folding.question: Which part of the orbit is folded?
folding.answer: The formula uses absolute coordinate magnitudes and folds the imaginary coordinate within the cross term.

julia-mode.question: Can Buffalo produce Julia sets?
julia-mode.answer: Yes. Fixing c and varying the starting point reveals connected and disconnected Buffalo Julia structures.

circle-inversion.title: Circle Inversion
circle-inversion.summary: A reciprocal quadratic map that sends small values far away and large values back toward the origin.

iteration.label: Reciprocal quadratic iteration
iteration.explanation: Each step takes the reciprocal of z squared before adding c.

circle-inversion.visualCharacteristics: Circular spines, nested rings, and sharp axial structures gather around the reciprocal singularity.

origin.question: Why is the origin special?
origin.answer: The reciprocal of z squared is undefined at zero, making the origin a pole of the map.

singularity.question: How does FractalPark handle values near zero?
singularity.answer: The renderer uses a small numerical safeguard while preserving the pole's visible influence on nearby orbits.

inverted-lambda.title: Inverted Lambda
inverted-lambda.summary: A hybrid map that adds a reciprocal quadratic term to the complex logistic recurrence.

iteration.label: Lambda-reciprocal iteration
iteration.explanation: The ordinary lambda term is combined with a reciprocal correction centered on z squared plus c.

inverted-lambda.visualCharacteristics: Knots, fault lines, and broken logistic lobes form around poles introduced by the reciprocal term.

inversion.question: What is inverted in this formula?
inversion.answer: A reciprocal term is added to the lambda map; the name describes that rational contribution rather than a view transform.

poles.question: Where can poles occur?
poles.answer: They occur where z squared plus c approaches zero.

mcmullen-2-3.title: McMullen 2–3 Map
mcmullen-2-3.summary: A rational map combining a quadratic term with an inverse cubic term.

iteration.label: McMullen 2–3 iteration
iteration.explanation: The map adds z squared to c divided by z cubed, balancing polynomial growth with a pole.

mcmullen-2-3.visualCharacteristics: Whorls, necklaces, and nested annular structures gather around a central reciprocal singularity.

exponents.question: What do 2 and 3 mean in the name?
exponents.answer: They are the exponents of the polynomial term z squared and the reciprocal term one over z cubed.

singularity.question: Why is z = 0 singular?
singularity.answer: The inverse cubic term divides by z cubed, so it has a pole at the origin.

rational-map-1.title: Rational Map 1
rational-map-1.summary: A compact rational iteration that divides z squared by z plus c.

iteration.label: Rational iteration
iteration.explanation: The quadratic numerator is reshaped by a moving denominator whose pole depends on c.

rational-map-1.visualCharacteristics: Fans, blades, and curved channels radiate from the map's parameter-dependent pole.

rational.question: What makes this a rational map?
rational.answer: Its iteration is a quotient of two complex polynomials rather than a polynomial alone.

spider.title: Spider
spider.summary: A rational quadratic hybrid that adds c divided by z to the familiar squared orbit.

iteration.label: Spider iteration
iteration.explanation: The reciprocal term pulls the quadratic orbit around a pole at zero.

spider.visualCharacteristics: Long legs, abyssal filaments, and web-like junctions radiate from narrow central structures.

zero.question: What happens at z = 0?
zero.answer: The reciprocal term is singular there, so the implementation uses a stable fallback for values extremely close to zero.

filaments.question: What creates the spider-like legs?
filaments.answer: The competition between quadratic expansion and reciprocal attraction stretches the boundary into long filaments.

zaslavsky-map.title: Zaslavsky Map
zaslavsky-map.summary: A complex sinusoidal map that combines a nonlinear swirl with a fixed rotation and translation.

iteration.label: Sinusoidal rotation map
iteration.explanation: A sine perturbation bends z, a fixed complex multiplier rotates it, and c translates the result.

zaslavsky-map.visualCharacteristics: Swirling arms and mandala-like rings become especially pronounced when paired with kaleidoscopic transforms.

rotation.question: Where does the rotation come from?
rotation.answer: The map multiplies the perturbed orbit by a unit complex number with angle 0.55 radians.

transform.question: Is kaleidoscope part of the formula?
transform.answer: No. Kaleidoscope is an optional spatial transform applied outside the formula iteration.

zubieta.title: Zubieta
zubieta.summary: A quadratic map that folds both components of z squared plus c into the nonnegative quadrant.

iteration.label: Component-folded iteration
iteration.explanation: After the quadratic step and addition of c, absolute value is applied separately to both components.

zubieta.visualCharacteristics: Mirrored wedges, compact mandalas, and tiled lobes reflect the strong component-wise fold.

absolute-value.question: Is the absolute value a complex magnitude?
absolute-value.answer: No. FractalPark applies absolute value separately to the real and imaginary components.

symmetry.question: Why is the image strongly mirrored?
symmetry.answer: Folding both output components into one quadrant repeatedly imposes multiple reflection symmetries.

preset-newton-deep-spiral.summary: A deep Newton-basin descent where three root regions twist into a compact spiral.
preset-newton-deep-spiral.visualNote: Fine alternating bands tighten toward the center while the rotated frame keeps the motion diagonal.

preset-lambda-julia-vortex.summary: A Lambda Julia vortex built from a long zoom into a folded boundary.
preset-lambda-julia-vortex.visualNote: Dark channels divide pale curved blades that seem to circulate around an off-center eye.

seo.heading: FractalPark Explorer — Free In-Browser Fractal Generator
seo.intro: FractalPark is a free, open-source (MIT) WebGL fractal generator that runs entirely in your browser. Explore 94 fractal formulas across 7 families — from the classic Mandelbrot and Julia sets to Burning Ship, Newton, Phoenix, and exotic transcendental attractors — and export high-resolution PNG images up to 4× without installing anything.
seo.howToHeading: How to Generate Your First Fractal
howToSteps: Pick a formula from the Formula tab — try the classic Mandelbrot set to start.
Drag on the canvas to pan, scroll to zoom into the boundary region where detail lives.
Switch to the Coloring tab and try smooth iteration, orbit traps, or a custom gradient.
Open the Render tab to enable anti-aliasing (SSAA) and adaptive iteration depth.
Click Export to download a high-resolution PNG, or Share to copy a link that restores the exact view.
seo.familiesIntro: Every formula is implemented in GLSL with both Mandelbrot and Julia modes. Click any formula name in the explorer to load it with sensible defaults.

features: 94 GLSL fractal formulas with Mandelbrot and Julia modes
7 coloring modes including smooth iteration, orbit traps, and custom gradients
Real-time WebGL rendering at 60 fps on any modern device
High-resolution PNG export up to 4× with SSAA anti-aliasing
Shareable URLs that restore the exact view and parameters
Custom formula editor with AST validation and live preview

about.title: About FractalPark
about.intro: FractalPark is an open-source fractal art generator that runs directly in your browser. You do not need to install anything: open the explorer, choose a formula, adjust the colors, and make a piece of mathematical art at your own pace.
about.aiDescription: FractalPark is an open-source MIT-licensed browser-based fractal art generator using WebGL for real-time GPU rendering. It features 94 built-in escape-time fractal formulas (Mandelbrot, Julia, Newton, Phoenix, Magnet, McMullen, rational, transcendental families), a custom formula editor with Fractint .frm syntax support, 7 UV transform plugins, 9 coloring modes, and high-resolution PNG export. Built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript 5, and Tailwind CSS. The rendering engine uses a plugin architecture with dynamic GLSL shader assembly and LRU caching.

techStack.rendering: Rendering: WebGL 1 (GLSL fragment shaders), plugin-based architecture, shader LRU cache
techStack.formula: Formula System: Custom Fractint .frm parser, CodeMirror 6 editor, AST-to-GLSL transpiler
techStack.deployment: Deployment: Vercel with Analytics and Speed Insights

vision.title: Vision
vision.description: We want fractal exploration to feel open, welcoming, and easy to start. Whether you are here to make an image, learn a bit of math, inspect the code, or remix the project, FractalPark should give you a friendly place to begin.
